strengths: Novel and simple optical design: uses only two off-the-shelf lenses and a grayscale sensor with a moving-lens chromatic focal sweep, avoiding coded apertures, dispersive elements, or DOEs, which reduces hardware complexity and cost relative to CASSI-like or diffractive spectral imagers.

Physics-based reconstruction (plug-and-play ADMM with eigenspace projection and a fast BCCB-based matrix inversion) achieves sub-second reconstruction, which is a substantial speed improvement over several competing optimization-based approaches (e.g., >15 min for SDC/Choi et al.).

State-of-the-art PSNR/SSIM on simulated benchmarks (Table 1, Fig. 3) with fewer optical components (4) than most alternatives, and mitigates hallucination artifacts common to purely data-driven methods like MST.

Real hardware prototype is built and validated with quantitative (Macbeth chart, ΔE00, SAM) and qualitative experiments, including robustness tests across working distance and number of measurements, which strengthens practical credibility beyond simulation.
Clear articulation of trade-offs and honest discussion of limitations (fixed PSF stack, restricted depth range, paraxial FOV, and the need for more measurements for RGB in dynamic settings).
weaknesses: SAM performance is only second-best (36.51° vs KRISM's 34.38°), and the method underperforms on the higher-wavelength range or under low SNR per the authors' own admission, raising questions about robustness of spectral accuracy in harder conditions.

Evaluation of real-world hardware is limited mostly to Macbeth charts and a handful of lab scenes/objects (toys, pinwheels); no large-scale quantitative benchmark on real data with diverse natural scenes, limiting evidence of generalizability outside controlled lab conditions.

The system requires targets to remain within a narrow depth of field (34 cm) and near the optical axis to avoid aberration-induced model mismatch, restricting applicability to scenes with meaningful depth variation—an important practical constraint not stress-tested extensively.

Because reconstruction relies on capturing multiple sequential lens positions (focal stack), it is inherently unsuitable for dynamic scenes without motion artifacts; the paper's frame-rate comparisons (Fig. 1a) still show relatively low fps for the method compared to conventional imaging even if it's the fastest of the alternatives compared.

Reliance on a fixed, pre-calibrated PSF stack specific to depth and target placement is a real limitation acknowledged in the conclusion but not quantitatively characterized against alternative depths/off-axis scenarios in the main results.

The comparison to real hardware baselines (KRISM, MST, etc.) is done in simulation only for Table 1 and Fig. 3 (using Harvard/KAIST/CAVE datasets), while some baseline systems were originally validated on real hardware; the direct simulated comparison may not perfectly reflect true relative performance on physical systems.

strengths: The paper builds and demonstrates a working real hardware prototype (two off-the-shelf lenses + grayscale sensor) rather than relying purely on simulation, which is a meaningful practical contribution.

The physics-based plug-and-play ADMM formulation with a fast BCCB-based matrix inversion is a sensible way to reduce reconstruction time relative to naive optimization-based CASSI-type solvers, and sub-second reconstruction is a genuine practical advantage over several baselines.

Table 1 and Figure 1 provide a reasonably clear comparison across modalities (spectral filter, dispersive element, chromatic aberration) in terms of PSNR/SSIM/SAM, compute time, FOV, and optical component count, giving useful context for where the method sits relative to prior art.

The paper explicitly compares to a similar chromatic-aberration approach (Zhan et al.) and shows a clear win in reconstruction robustness under noise, which supports the claim that a data-driven inverse filtering approach is fragile while the proposed physics-based iterative algorithm is more robust.

The synthetic experiments span three public hyperspectral datasets with a physically motivated photon-noise model and a fixed total-exposure-time protocol, which is a fairer comparison setup than raw PSNR at arbitrary exposure.
weaknesses: Real-data quantitative evaluation is limited essentially to a single Macbeth color chart experiment (Figs. 4-5); there is no quantitative real-scene benchmark against ground-truth hyperspectral captures or against competing real hardware systems, which considerably weakens the empirical support for the 'state-of-the-art' claim in a real deployment setting.

The reported average ΔE00 color difference (3.77) is explicitly acknowledged to be above the perceptual-equivalence threshold of 2, undercutting the color-accuracy claims even in the best-case, well-controlled lab test.

The method's SAM (spectral angle) metric is worse than KRISM in Table 1, and the paper's explanation (KRISM does SVD in-scene) reads as a post hoc justification rather than a substantive analysis of why the proposed approach underperforms on this specific and important spectral-fidelity metric.

The system has significant deployment constraints: an assumed narrow depth of field (34 cm) with defocus effects outside this range explicitly not modeled, a fixed working distance calibration, and a requirement that targets be centered near the optical axis to avoid chromatic/spherical aberration artifacts—these are non-trivial practical restrictions understated in the main claims of a 'fast, compact, general' HSI solution.

The core physical principle (using longitudinal chromatic aberration/focal sweeps of simple lenses to encode spectral information) has substantial overlap with prior works cited in the paper itself (Zhan et al., Cossairt & Nayar, Huang et al.), so the central novelty appears to lie mainly in the specific reconstruction algorithm (eigenspace + PnP-ADMM + BCCB fast inversion) rather than in the imaging concept itself; the paper could more clearly delineate this incremental contribution.

The method requires more than 3 measurements to produce usable RGB output and reconstruction quality/robustness depends on measurement count (Fig. 5b, Fig. 6), yet the headline frame-rate/compute-time comparisons in Fig. 1 and Table 1 do not fully make transparent how much quality is sacrificed at the low measurement counts used for the fastest reported frame rates.

Some qualitative real results (Fig. 6) show visible false-color/spatial artifacts with only 3 measurements, and the fix (adding more measurements) is presented somewhat briefly without a systematic study of the artifact mechanism or a principled stopping criterion.

The regularizer relies on an off-the-shelf deep denoiser trained on separate hyperspectral image data, which reintroduces a data-driven / learned component into a method whose main selling point is being 'physics-based' and less prone to hallucination than fully data-driven baselines; the extent to which this denoiser can itself hallucinate or generalize poorly to real captured noise statistics is not analyzed.

strengths: Presents a physically well-motivated and simple hardware design (two off-the-shelf lenses + grayscale sensor) that exploits naturally occurring longitudinal chromatic aberration rather than requiring custom DOEs, coded apertures, or dispersive elements, substantially reducing optical complexity (4 components vs up to 20 in prior systems).

Strong quantitative results: achieves best PSNR/SSIM among compared SOTA methods (Table 1, Fig. 3) with competitive SAM and much faster reconstruction (0.64s) than several optimization-based baselines (>15 min for SDC and Choi et al.), while being more light-efficient than tunable-filter/coded-aperture designs.

The reconstruction algorithm is a well-derived physics-based plug-and-play ADMM formulation with a low-dimensional eigenspace projection and a fast matrix inversion (BCCB structure) that is both interpretable and efficient, avoiding the hallucination artifacts noted in purely data-driven approaches (MST, Choi et al.) as documented via specific spectral examples (e.g., metameric fake vs real object discrimination in Fig. 3).

Real hardware prototype was built and validated (not just simulation), with Macbeth color chart evaluation, robustness studies across depth-plane distance and number of measurements, and qualitative real-scene reconstructions (Figs. 4-6), lending credibility to practical applicability.
Clear ablation-style analysis of how the number of measurements trades off against reconstruction quality (Fig. 5b) and depth robustness (Fig. 5a), giving useful practical guidance.
Honest discussion of limitations (fixed PSF stack, limited depth/FOV, need for >3 measurements for HSI) in the conclusion rather than overstating generality.
weaknesses: The synthetic comparison is conducted under a specific brightly lit condition (photon flux, 5s total exposure) and it is unclear how sensitive relative rankings are to different noise/illumination regimes; only one operating point is thoroughly explored quantitatively for the synthetic benchmark.

Real-data quantitative evaluation is limited essentially to a single Macbeth color chart at fixed distance (with some distance/measurement-count robustness checks), and the average ΔE00 of 3.77 is above the perceptual threshold of 2, indicating non-negligible real-world color error that is somewhat brushed aside as 'likely to go unnoticed in practice' without stronger justification or user study.

Field of view and depth of field are quite restricted (paraxial FOV, 34 cm DoF, fixed working distance ~2.8 m), and the system requires the target to remain within a narrow depth range with careful centering to avoid spherical/chromatic aberration effects — these are acknowledged but may substantially limit real-world applicability beyond lab conditions.

The number of measurements needed (5-10) for good spectral accuracy, while lower than many scanning systems, means the system is not truly single-shot; dynamic scene capability is explicitly deferred as future work, so claims of 'fast' imaging apply mainly to static or slow scenes.

Some qualitative real results (Fig. 6, 3-measurement case) show visible spatial/spectral artifacts (false color patterns), and it's not fully clear how robust the method is to scene content outside the calibrated targets (textures, natural scenes) versus the curated test objects shown.

Reproducibility could be aided by more explicit detail in the main text on calibration procedure sensitivity and computational cost breakdown, though this is likely covered in the supplement, which was not provided for review.

strengths: Novel and elegant use of naturally occurring chromatic aberration from two off-the-shelf lenses as an implicit spectral encoder, avoiding custom-fabricated diffractive/dispersive optics, prisms, or coded apertures used in most compressive HSI systems.

Strong empirical results: Table 1 and Fig. 3 show SfD achieves best or near-best PSNR/SSIM/SAM among 9 compared methods across multiple modalities (spectral filter, dispersive, diffractive, chromatic aberration), while using far fewer optical components (only 4-5) and sub-second reconstruction time on an RTX A6000.

Physically interpretable forward model (Eq. 1) combined with a plug-and-play ADMM algorithm that leverages a low-rank spectral eigenbasis and a BCCB-based fast matrix inversion, giving a principled, data-efficient combination of physics-based and learned (deep denoiser) priors rather than a purely black-box network.

Demonstrated advantages in photon efficiency and robustness under low-light/short-exposure conditions (Fig. 3b), which is a practically important regime for many real hyperspectral applications and is a differentiator versus filter-based and dispersive competitors that show severe degradation or hallucination.

Real hardware prototype validation (Sec. 4.3-4.4, Figs. 4-5) with LCTF ground truth comparison, Macbeth color checker spectral accuracy quantification (~29.5 dB PSNR, 7.4° SAM), and an explicit working-range/robustness analysis (Fig. 5) rather than relying solely on simulation.

Clear ablation/comparison across a wide taxonomy of competing HSI paradigms (scanning, spectral filter, CASSI/dispersive, DOE, chromatic aberration) giving good contextualization of the contribution within the field.
weaknesses: The evaluation, while broad in comparison methods, is limited in scene diversity for real data: only four real prototype scenes and one Macbeth chart are shown; conclusions about generalization to complex real-world scenes with fine spectral texture remain somewhat under-supported.

The system assumes a narrow, fixed working depth range (~34 cm) and explicitly acknowledges failures/artifacts outside this range and at long wavelengths (Sec. 5, Fig. 5b); this practical limitation (needing known/controlled scene depth) is a meaningful constraint on real-world applicability that is only partially quantified.

The low-rank spectral prior (via PCA basis B from the Harvard dataset) could bias reconstructions toward statistics of the calibration dataset; the paper acknowledges spectral oversmoothing/color bleeding but does not deeply analyze failure modes on out-of-distribution spectra (e.g., narrowband emission lines, fluorescent sources).

Static-scene, multi-shot (5-exposure) capture requirement limits applicability to dynamic scenes; the paper defers full treatment of motion robustness to future work, so the "fast spectral imaging" claim in the title is somewhat qualified by the need for a focal sweep across 5 positions requiring mechanical actuation, which is not conclusively shown to be fast/robust in dynamic settings.

Some reported failure cases (e.g., pinwheel pattern at 700 nm, red/black color desaturation) suggest that photometric/spatial resolution can degrade for high-contrast or saturated-color test patterns, and the explanation given (confusion between defocus and true darkness) points to a fairly fundamental ambiguity in the single-grayscale-sensor design that may not be fully solvable by better priors alone.

The paper is dense and the ADMM/algorithmic derivation is deferred largely to supplementary material, making full reproducibility and complete understanding of hyperparameter choices (e.g., mu1, mu2, convergence criteria specifics) dependent on materials not included in the main manuscript.

strengths: A genuinely simple, low-cost optical design (only two off-the-shelf lenses plus a grayscale sensor) that achieves competitive or state-of-the-art PSNR/SSIM/SAM against a wide range of much more complex optical systems (dispersive elements, DOEs, coded apertures), as shown in Table 1 and Fig. 3.

The physics-based forward model (Eq. 1) combined with a plug-and-play ADMM solver operating in a low-rank spectral eigenspace is a reasonable, interpretable way to combine model-based and data-driven priors, and is shown to reduce the hallucination artifacts that purely data-driven baselines (e.g., MST) exhibit under low light (Fig. 3b).

A fast matrix-inversion strategy exploiting the Block-Circulant-with-Circulant-Blocks structure of the convolution operator enables sub-second reconstruction, which is a meaningful practical advantage over classical iterative solvers.

The paper backs its simulation results with an actual hardware prototype and real captured data (Fig. 4), including calibration against ground-truth LCTF spectral images and Macbeth color-checker quantitative evaluation, which strengthens the credibility of the claims beyond simulation alone.

The paper is reasonably transparent about limitations: it explicitly analyzes and reports degraded performance outside the assumed depth working range and narrow field of view (Fig. 5), rather than hiding these constraints.
weaknesses: The method requires sequential capture at 5 discrete lens positions to build the focal stack; despite the abstract's framing as 'fast' and suited to 'low-photon, dynamic conditions,' this multi-shot acquisition is not actually simultaneous, and the paper's own conclusion admits that motion in dynamic scenes is an unresolved issue, undercutting the dynamic-scene motivation stated in the introduction.

The reconstruction relies on a low-rank spectral prior (top eigenvectors from PCA on the Harvard dataset) baked into the projection operator P; this raises concerns about generalization to spectra with significant high-frequency structure or scenes statistically different from the training/calibration data, an issue the paper itself flags only briefly (oversmoothing in Fig. 3c, spectral bias risk).

The claimed working volume is narrow (34 cm depth of field, ~10° FOV cropped from a much larger sensor), which is a substantial practical limitation for a technique proposed as a general-purpose hyperspectral imaging solution; while acknowledged, this materially limits the claimed applicability to real-world unconstrained scenes.

Real-world validation is limited to a small number of curated scenes (toys, color charts, a book), with no outdoor, natural, or genuinely dynamic scene results, despite the paper motivating itself around scenarios like remote sensing, food inspection, and dynamic/low-light conditions.

Real prototype results show a clear qualitative failure mode (e.g., pinwheel/high-frequency-pattern reconstruction failure at 700 nm), attributed to sensor dynamic range and ambiguity between defocused bright and true dark regions; this is a nontrivial, unresolved artifact rather than a minor presentation issue.

The fairness of cross-method comparisons in Table 1/Fig. 3 depends on assumptions about equalized total exposure time and photon budget across very different optical architectures (dispersive, DOE, filter-based); such normalization is difficult to fully validate and could bias comparisons in the proposed method's favor.

Conceptual novelty is somewhat incremental: exploiting chromatic aberration for spectral encoding and using focal sweeps has been explored in prior work (e.g., Cossairt & Nayar's chromatic focal sweep, DefocusCam, Zhan et al.); the core contribution is largely a new combination of an existing physical cue with a specific PnP-ADMM low-rank algorithm rather than a fundamentally new principle.

strengths: The core idea—exploiting naturally occurring longitudinal chromatic aberration from a pair of off-the-shelf refractive lenses combined with a focal sweep to encode spectral information—is simple, elegant, and avoids custom-fabricated optics (DOEs, metasurfaces, dispersive elements, coded apertures) that are typically required in compressive spectral imaging.

The physics-based forward model (block-convolutional operator built from measured PSFs at each focal position) combined with a plug-and-play ADMM reconstruction using a low-rank spectral eigenspace and a fast BCCB-based matrix inversion is well-motivated and yields sub-second reconstruction, addressing a genuine practical bottleneck of prior iterative/optimization-based hyperspectral reconstruction methods.

The paper reports a thorough comparison against 8 other methods spanning very different modalities (spectral filter, dispersive element, diffractive element, chromatic aberration) on standard datasets (Harvard, KAIST, CAVE) with multiple metrics (PSNR, SSIM, SAM), and also demonstrates low-light/low-exposure robustness, which is a compelling practical advantage given the motivation about photon efficiency.

A real hardware prototype was built and validated against LCTF ground truth on real scenes (not just simulation), including quantitative PSNR/SAM per Macbeth patch and qualitative reconstructions of natural objects, lending credibility to the claimed real-world applicability.

The paper includes an honest discussion of limitations (narrow depth of field/working range, degraded performance for black/saturated regions, dependence on scene occupying assumed low-rank spectral subspace, need for higher-fidelity noise models at very low light), which strengthens scientific rigor and transparency.

Optical simplicity (2 lenses + grayscale sensor, only 4 optical components) compared to systems with up to 20 components is a meaningful practical/engineering contribution for cost and complexity reduction.
weaknesses: The system has a narrow working depth range (~34 cm) with a fixed focal working distance (targets placed at 2.8 m); this substantially limits practicality for general/dynamic scenes, and while acknowledged, the severity of this constraint (versus e.g. dispersive systems) is not deeply quantified relative to real deployment scenarios.

Ground truth for real data is captured with an LCTF requiring 29 sequential exposures per scene, meaning the real-data experiments are effectively static-scene validations; no dynamic-scene or truly snapshot demonstration is shown despite motivating claims about fast/short-exposure imaging.

Only N=5 focal positions/measurements are used, and while claimed sufficient, the paper does not clearly justify why 5 is optimal versus a systematic study of the accuracy/speed/measurement-count trade-off in the main text (partially deferred to supplement).

The reconstruction relies on a low-rank spectral prior learned from the Harvard dataset (matrix P), which could bias performance for spectra outside this training distribution (e.g., narrow-band illuminants, fluorescent/industrial materials); generalization to out-of-distribution spectra is not directly assessed.

Several key implementation and justification details (PSF calibration procedure robustness, sensitivity to lens/sensor alignment tolerances, computation of μ1/μ2, comparison methodology fairness across drastically different optical setups) are deferred to supplementary material not included in the main manuscript, making some claims difficult to fully verify from the paper alone.

The comparison table normalizes total exposure time across modalities, but real-world deployment differences (e.g., mechanical stability of a moving lens versus static coded-aperture systems, calibration overhead) are not quantitatively compared, which could affect the practical significance of claimed advantages.
